Let’s dive into Chapter 4—Building New Habits: Making Coaching a Consistent Practice.
You know, adopting a coaching mindset isn’t just something you do once and forget about. It’s really about building new habits—shaping the way you show up for yourself and your team every single day.
Think about habits for a second. They’re like the invisible architecture of our daily lives. They quietly guide how we respond to challenges, how we connect with others, and even how we make decisions. If you want coaching to become a natural part of your leadership style, it helps to understand how these habits actually form—and, more importantly, how you can change them.
At the heart of every habit is a simple loop. There’s a trigger, a behavior, and then a reward. Picture this: A team member walks up with a problem. That’s your trigger. Without even thinking, you jump in and offer advice—that’s the behavior. Instantly, there’s a sense of satisfaction when you help solve the issue—the reward. Do this enough times, and it just becomes automatic.
But what if you want to shift from giving advice to really coaching? You’ve got to break that loop.
Here’s how:
First, start by identifying the trigger. Notice those moments when you feel that urge to jump in with answers.
Next, choose a new behavior. Instead of handing out advice, try asking a coaching question. Something like, “What ideas do you have for tackling this?”
And finally, notice the reward. Pay attention to the positive shift—maybe your team is more engaged, or you see someone’s confidence grow.
Now, let’s be real—changing old habits isn’t always easy. The instinct to help can be pretty strong, and old patterns run deep. But with a little practice and some intention, you can build new habits that stick.
One tip? Start small. Pick just one or two coaching questions and use them regularly, until they feel totally natural.
Another powerful tool is self-reflection. After each coaching conversation, take a moment to ask yourself—what went well? What could be better next time? These small check-ins help you grow and keep the learning alive.
Remember, you don’t have to go it alone. Sharing your goal to build a coaching habit with a colleague or mentor can keep you accountable and give you that nudge of encouragement when you need it. And don’t forget to celebrate the wins—no matter how small! Every step counts.
When coaching becomes a shared habit in an organization, the benefits are huge. Teams get stronger, more adaptable, and more creative. Leaders stop feeling like they need to have all the answers, and employees feel empowered to take initiative and solve problems on their own.
So, here’s the key takeaway: Building a coaching habit is a journey, not a destination. It takes patience and persistence, and you’ll learn from both your wins and your setbacks. But the rewards? They’re worth it—stronger relationships, more engaged teams, and a culture where everyone’s learning and growing together.
